x: Overview # Highly intelligent and able to recognise individual humans in aquaria. Each arm has ~280 suckers. Habitat and type of water # North Pacific coasts from Japan to California, intertidal to ~2,000 m. Feeding and hunting # Forages at night, drilling or prying open shellfish and leaving shell middens outside its den. Mating and reproduction # The male passes sperm with a modified arm (hectocotylus). The female lays up to ~100,000 eggs in a den and guards them without eating for ~6 months, then dies. Movement and migration # Moves to deeper water in winter in some regions. Behaviour and social life # Solitary, den-living, masters of camouflage. Adaptations # Colour-changing chromatophores Distributed nervous system with neurons in the arms Conservation # Targeted by small fisheries.

x: Overview # Architeuthis has the largest eyes in the animal kingdom (~27 cm), likely for spotting the bioluminescent wakes of approaching sperm whales. Feeding and hunting # Hunts fish and squid, seizing prey with two long feeding tentacles lined with toothed suckers. Mating and reproduction # Males have a long muscular penis and inject sperm packets into the female’s arms. Eggs are probably released in gelatinous masses. Movement and migration # Not well known. Behaviour and social life # Solitary. A key prey of sperm whales, which bear sucker scars from fights. Adaptations # Giant eyes Ammonium-rich tissues for buoyancy Toothed sucker rings Conservation # Not fished commercially.

d: Neither squid nor octopus: a gentle detritus eater living in the oxygen minimum zone.
x: Overview # The sole surviving member of its order. Despite its name it is not predatory: it collects marine snow with two retractile filaments and mucus. Habitat and type of water # Tropical and temperate oceans in oxygen minimum zones, 600–1,200 m. Feeding and hunting # Gathers sinking organic particles with sticky filaments and rolls them into mucus balls to eat. Mating and reproduction # Unusually for cephalopods, it appears to spawn multiple times over its life, with resting phases between. Movement and migration # Stays within the oxygen minimum zone, where few predators can follow. Behaviour and social life # When threatened it turns its webbed cloak inside out (‘pineapple posture’) and ejects glowing mucus instead of ink. Adaptations # Haemocyanin that binds oxygen efficiently in low-oxygen water Very low metabolic rate Bioluminescent arm tips Conservation # Not threatened. d: Lanternfish with a large headlight photophore.
The classic deep-sea anglerfish: a lure of glowing bacteria, a cavernous mouth and dwarf males.
x: Overview # A black, globe-shaped predator of the bathypelagic zone and one of the most recognisable deep-sea animals. Females carry a fishing-rod lure (illicium) tipped with a light organ (esca) packed with symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria. Habitat and type of water # Open water of the midnight zone worldwide in tropical to temperate seas, mostly 1,000–2,000 m, recorded from ~200 to ~4,500 m. Feeding and hunting # A sit-and-wait ambush predator. It hangs motionless and wiggles its glowing lure to draw prey close, then engulfs it. Its stomach and jaws expand so it can swallow prey as large as itself, which matters where meals are rare. Mating and reproduction # Males are tiny and free-swimming, with large nostrils for tracking female pheromones. In Melanocetus the male attaches temporarily to the female; in some other anglerfish families males fuse permanently (sexual parasitism). Eggs are released in buoyant gelatinous veils, and larvae develop in shallower water. Movement and migration # Larvae and juveniles live higher in the water column and descend as they mature (ontogenetic migration). Adults do not migrate daily. Behaviour and social life # Solitary, energy-saving and largely motionless. Encounters between the sexes are rare, which is why mate-finding adaptations are so extreme. Adaptations # Bacterial bioluminescent lure Distensible stomach and hinged jaws Black, light-absorbing skin Weak, watery muscles that save energy Conservation # Not commercially fished. The main threats are indirect (deep-sea trawling bycatch, climate-driven changes in food supply).

d: Caught at 8,022 m, the deepest fish ever captured.

x: Overview # About 250 species of small fish covered in photophores (light organs) in species-specific patterns. Together they may make up a large share of the global fish biomass, and they underpin food webs for tuna, squid, seabirds and marine mammals. Habitat and type of water # Every ocean, mesopelagic zone by day (300–1,500 m), near-surface by night. Feeding and hunting # Feed at night near the surface on copepods, krill and other zooplankton, then descend at dawn to digest in dark, cold water safe from visual predators. Mating and reproduction # Broadcast spawners with pelagic eggs and larvae. Many species mature within a year, and their short lives support rapid population turnover. Movement and migration # Diel vertical migration: hundreds of metres up at dusk and down at dawn, every day. This transports carbon to depth (the ‘migrant pump’). Behaviour and social life # Schooling. Photophores on the belly provide counter-illumination, matching downwelling light to hide the fish’s silhouette from predators below. Adaptations # Ventral photophores for counter-illumination Large eyes tuned to blue light Gas-filled or lipid-filled swim bladders (varies by species) Conservation # Targeted by small experimental fisheries for fishmeal. Scientists caution that large-scale twilight-zone fishing could weaken the ocean’s carbon pump.

Feeding and hunting # Feeds on abundant amphipods by suction. In the hadal zone there are few competing fish predators. Mating and reproduction # Lays relatively large eggs. Juveniles of hadal snailfishes tend to live deepest within the species’ range. Movement and migration # Lives within a narrow trench depth band. Behaviour and social life # Active swimmers that gather at baited cameras in groups. Adaptations # No swim bladder Incompletely ossified skull High TMAO levels to stabilise proteins under pressure Gelatinous tissue Conservation # Not fished. Trenches accumulate pollutants and microplastics.

Habitat and type of water # Cold deep waters of the Atlantic, Indo-Pacific and especially around New Zealand and Australia, often over seamounts. Feeding and hunting # Feeds on mesopelagic prey drawn to seamounts by currents. Mating and reproduction # Forms dense spawning aggregations, which made it easy to catch in very large quantities. Fecundity is low for its size. Movement and migration # Moves between feeding and spawning grounds on seamounts. Behaviour and social life # Aggregates in large schools around seamounts. Adaptations # Extremely slow metabolism and growth Long lifespan Conservation # Many stocks were heavily overfished in the 1980s–90s. Bottom trawling on seamounts also destroyed coral habitat. Some stocks have since been rebuilt under strict management.

It stretches about 15,500 km from the Bering Strait to Antarctica and nearly 20,000 km from Indonesia to Colombia. Its name, ‘peaceful sea’, came from Magellan in 1520, but it is the most geologically violent ocean, ringed by the Ring of Fire. Its tropical belt generates the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the most important source of year-to-year climate variability on the planet. Geography # Bounded by Asia and Australia to the west, the Americas to the east and the Southern Ocean to the south (about 60°S). Marginal seas include the Bering, Okhotsk, Japan, Yellow, East and South China, Philippine, Coral and Tasman seas. More than 25,000 islands lie in the Pacific, more than in all other oceans combined, grouped into Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia. Seafloor and geology # The Pacific plate is the largest tectonic plate and is being consumed at subduction zones on almost every side. That creates the deepest trenches on Earth: Mariana (Challenger Deep, ~10,935 m), Tonga (~10,800 m), Philippine, Kuril–Kamchatka, Kermadec and Japan trenches. The East Pacific Rise spreads up to ~15 cm a year, the fastest on Earth, and hosts black-smoker vents. Tens of thousands of seamounts and guyots dot the basin, including the Hawaiian–Emperor chain that records the plate’s motion over a hotspot. The Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico holds the world’s richest polymetallic nodule fields. Water and currents # Two great gyres (North and South Pacific) circulate clockwise and anticlockwise. The Kuroshio is the Pacific’s Gulf Stream; the California and Humboldt currents carry cold water toward the equator and drive rich upwelling. The tropical Pacific warm pool is the warmest large body of ocean water. Every 2–7 years El Niño weakens the trade winds and warms the eastern Pacific, while La Niña does the opposite; the swings shift rainfall, cyclones and fisheries worldwide. The eastern tropical Pacific holds the largest oxygen minimum zone in the ocean. Climate, weather and cyclones # The western North Pacific produces more tropical cyclones (typhoons) than any other basin, about a third of the global total, including the strongest storms on record. El Niño years bring floods to Peru, drought to Australia and Indonesia, and weaker Indian monsoons. The Pacific Decadal Oscillation shifts sea temperatures over decades, and the 2014–16 ‘Blob’ marine heatwave killed seabirds, whales and kelp along North America. Flora and fauna # The Coral Triangle (Indonesia, Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands) holds about 76% of all known coral species and the world’s richest reef fish diversity. d: The second-largest ocean, split down the middle by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and home to the AMOC.
x: Overview # The Atlantic is the second-largest ocean (about 106 million km²) and the youngest of the major basins, opening as Pangaea broke apart around 180 million years ago. It is still widening by about 2.5 cm a year along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. It is the saltiest open ocean and the engine room of the global overturning circulation: cold, salty water sinks in the north and spreads through the deep ocean worldwide. That makes the Atlantic central to Earth’s climate. Geography # An S-shaped basin between the Americas to the west and Europe and Africa to the east, from the Arctic to the Southern Ocean. Marginal seas include the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Mediterranean, North, Baltic, Norwegian and Labrador seas, plus the Sargasso Sea, the only sea with no coastline. It drains more river water than any other ocean, including the Amazon, Congo, Mississippi and Niger. Seafloor and geology # The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs ~16,000 km down the centre and rises above sea level in Iceland and the Azores. Vent fields such as TAG, Rainbow and the alkaline Lost City lie along it. The deepest point is the Milwaukee Deep in the Puerto Rico Trench (~8,376 m); the South Sandwich Trench lies in the far south. Wide continental shelves (Grand Banks, North Sea, Patagonian shelf) host rich fisheries, and submarine canyons cut the margins. Water and currents # The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Current carry tropical heat to Europe. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) sinks water in the Labrador and Nordic seas, forming North Atlantic Deep Water. In the south, the Benguela upwelling off Namibia is one of the most productive systems on Earth. Salinity reaches ~37 PSU in the subtropics because evaporation exceeds rainfall. Climate, weather and cyclones # The tropical Atlantic produces hurricanes from June to November, born from African easterly waves over warm water above ~26.5°C. The North Atlantic Oscillation steers European winters. A weakening AMOC is one of the major climate tipping-point concerns (see AMOC weakening). Flora and fauna # Cold-water coral reefs off Norway and Ireland, the cod and herring stocks of the Grand Banks and North Sea, North Atlantic right whales, humpbacks breeding in the Caribbean, Atlantic bluefin tuna crossing the basin, the Sargasso Sea’s floating sargassum community where European and American eels spawn, sea turtles, gannets, puffins, and the Lost City vent fauna. Ecosystems # Sargassum mats, coral reefs (Caribbean), cold-water coral mounds, seagrass and mangroves, upwelling systems (Benguela, Canary), vent and seep communities, and the abyssal plains of the Cape Verde and Sohm basins. History and exploration # Vikings reached North America around 1000 CE; Columbus crossed in 1492. The Atlantic slave trade forcibly carried over 12 million Africans across it. Matthew Maury charted its winds and currents in the 1850s; the first transatlantic telegraph cable was laid in 1858. Famous wrecks include the Titani

d: The warmest ocean, ruled by monsoon reversals of winds and currents.
x: Overview # The Indian Ocean (~70.5 million km²) is the third-largest and the warmest ocean. Unlike the Pacific and Atlantic, it is closed to the north by Asia, so it has no northern polar water. Instead its circulation is ruled by the monsoon: winds and major currents reverse direction twice a year. It is named after India, whose rainfall, agriculture and economy depend directly on its behaviour. Geography # Bounded by Africa to the west, Asia to the north, Australia and Indonesia to the east and the Southern Ocean to the south. Marginal seas include the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, Andaman Sea, Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Laccadive Sea and Mozambique Channel. Island groups include Madagascar, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Lakshadweep, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Seychelles, Mauritius and Réunion. Major rivers include the Ganges–Brahmaputra, Indus, Zambezi and Irrawaddy. Seafloor and geology # The Java (Sunda) Trench (~7,290 m) is its deepest point and the source of the 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake and tsunami. Three ridges (Central, Southwest and Southeast Indian ridges) meet at the Rodrigues Triple Junction, where the Kairei vent field hosts the scaly-foot snail. The Bengal Fan, built by sediment from the Himalaya via the Ganges–Brahmaputra, is the largest submarine fan on Earth. The Central Indian Ocean Basin holds nodule fields explored by India under an ISA contract. Water and currents # During the southwest monsoon (June–September) the Somali Current flows north at up to ~3.5 m/s and drives strong upwelling off Somalia, Oman and western India; in the northeast monsoon it reverses. The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), a see-saw of temperatures between west and east, shapes rainfall in India, East Africa and Australia. The Agulhas Current, one of the strongest western boundary currents, leaks warm salty water into the Atlantic. The Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal hold intense oxygen minimum zones. Climate, weather and cyclones # The Bay of Bengal produces some of the deadliest tropical cyclones in history, because a shallow, funnel-shaped bay amplifies storm surges onto the low Ganges delta. Arabian Sea cyclones have become more frequent and intense as it warms. Monsoon rain from the ocean supplies most of India’s annual rainfall. The Indian Ocean is warming faster than any other ocean, intensifying marine heatwaves. Flora and fauna # Coelacanths off South Africa and Comoros, whale sharks of the Maldives and Ningaloo, dugongs, olive ridley turtles mass-nesting in Odisha, the Sundarbans mangroves with their tigers and Ganges river dolphins, manta rays of the Maldives, hilsa migrating up the Bengal rivers, and vent fauna like the scaly-foot snail. Ecosystems # Coral atolls (Maldives, Lakshadweep, Chagos), the Sundarbans (the world’s largest mangrove forest), seagrass meadows grazed by dugongs, upwelling systems, deep oxygen minimum zones and hydrothermal vents. History and exploration # Monsoon winds powered trade between Africa, Arabia, Indi

d: The ring of ocean around Antarctica, driven by the strongest current on Earth.
x: Overview # The Southern Ocean encircles Antarctica south of about 60°S and was formally recognised as the fifth ocean by the International Hydrographic Organization in 2000 (and by National Geographic in 2021). It is defined less by coastlines than by a current: the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the largest current on Earth. It is the ocean’s main gateway between surface and deep water, absorbing a large share of the heat and carbon dioxide that humans add to the climate system. Geography # Surrounds Antarctica, with the Weddell, Ross, Amundsen, Bellingshausen and Scotia seas as major embayments. The Drake Passage between South America and the Antarctic Peninsula is its narrowest point. Sub-Antarctic islands such as South Georgia, Kerguelen, Heard and Macquarie are wildlife strongholds. Seafloor and geology # The South Sandwich Trench (~7,400 m, the Factorian Deep) is the deepest point. Continental shelves around Antarctica are unusually deep (~500 m) because the weight of the ice sheet pushes the crust down. Mid-ocean ridges and seamounts steer the circumpolar current. Water and currents # The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows eastward around the continent, carrying over 100 times the flow of all the world’s rivers. Antarctic Bottom Water, the densest water in the ocean, forms on the Weddell and Ross shelves as sea ice forms and rejects salt, then spreads along the floor of all oceans. Upwelling of old deep water around Antarctica brings nutrients and CO₂ back to the surface. Climate, weather and cyclones # Westerly winds are the strongest on Earth (‘Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Screaming Sixties’). Sea ice expands each winter to about 18 million km² and shrinks to ~3 million km² in summer; record lows since 2016, and especially 2023, have alarmed scientists. Warm water reaching beneath ice shelves (Thwaites, Pine Island) threatens future sea-level rise. Flora and fauna # Antarctic krill (perhaps the largest biomass of any wild animal species), emperor, Adélie, chinstrap, gentoo and king penguins, Weddell, leopard and crabeater seals, blue, humpback, fin and minke whales, albatrosses and petrels, and icefish with no red blood cells. Benthic communities include giant sea spiders and slow-growing sponges. Ecosystems # Sea-ice ecosystems (algae under ice), krill-based food webs, sub-Antarctic island seabird and seal colonies, deep continental shelves, and the ice-shelf cavities beneath floating ice. History and exploration # Cook crossed the Antarctic Circle in 1773. Sealers and whalers devastated fur seals and great whales in the 19th and 20th centuries. The Antarctic Treaty (1959) set the continent aside for peace and science; CCAMLR (1982) manages its marine life. Shackleton’s Endurance sank in the Weddell Sea in 1915 and was found at 3,008 m in 2022. People and economy # Krill and toothfish fisheries regulated by CCAMLR; tourism to the Antarctic Peninsula; research stations from about 30 nations, including

d: The smallest, shallowest ocean, losing its summer sea ice fast.
x: Overview # The Arctic is the smallest (~15.6 million km²) and shallowest ocean, mostly enclosed by Eurasia and North America. Much of it is covered by sea ice that grows and shrinks with the seasons. It is warming about four times faster than the global average, so its ice cover is one of the clearest signals of climate change. Geography # Ringed by Russia, Norway, Greenland, Canada and Alaska. Marginal seas include the Barents, Kara, Laptev, East Siberian, Chukchi and Beaufort seas, plus Baffin Bay and Hudson Bay. The Fram Strait is the main deep connection to the Atlantic; the narrow Bering Strait links it to the Pacific. Seafloor and geology # The Arctic has the widest continental shelves on Earth, especially off Siberia, holding about half its area. The Lomonosov Ridge divides it into the Amerasian and Eurasian basins; the Gakkel Ridge is the slowest-spreading ridge on Earth yet hosts active vents (the Aurora field). The deepest point is the Molloy Deep (~5,550 m) in the Fram Strait. Water and currents # The Beaufort Gyre stores fresh water from rivers and melting ice, and the Transpolar Drift carries ice from Siberia toward Fram Strait. Huge Siberian rivers (Ob, Yenisei, Lena) make the surface fresher than any other ocean. Atlantic water entering through the Barents Sea is warming the Arctic from below (‘Atlantification’). Climate, weather and cyclones # September sea-ice extent has fallen by about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979, and multi-year ice has largely disappeared. Loss of white ice exposes dark water that absorbs more sunlight, accelerating warming (ice–albedo feedback). Thawing subsea permafrost may release methane. Flora and fauna # Polar bears, walruses, ringed and bearded seals, narwhals, belugas and bowhead whales, polar cod living in ice cracks, ice algae, Arctic char, little auks and ivory gulls. The Bering and Barents seas host some of the richest fisheries on Earth. Ecosystems # Sea-ice ecosystems, polynyas (open-water oases in ice), shallow Siberian shelves, the Barents Sea cod system and vents on the Gakkel Ridge. History and exploration # Inuit and other Indigenous peoples have lived along its coasts for millennia. Searches for the Northwest Passage killed Franklin’s 1845 expedition; its ships Erebus and Terror were found in 2014 and 2016. Nansen’s Fram drifted across it in 1893–96; the submarine USS Nautilus passed under the North Pole in 1958. People and economy # Indigenous subsistence hunting, Barents Sea and Bering Sea fisheries, Arctic shipping routes opening as ice melts (the Northern Sea Route), and oil and gas exploration. Threats and protection # Rapid ice loss, Atlantification, shipping and oil-spill risk, microplastics trapped in sea ice, and fisheries moving north into unregulated waters (a central Arctic fishing moratorium was agreed in 2018).

d: A nearly enclosed sea with unusually warm, salty deep water and a long human history.
x: Overview # A nearly enclosed sea of about 2.5 million km² linking Europe, Africa and Asia, connected to the Atlantic only by the 14 km-wide Strait of Gibraltar. It is a remnant of the ancient Tethys Ocean and has been the stage for Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Arab, Venetian and Ottoman sea power for 4,000 years. Because evaporation exceeds river input, it is saltier and warmer than the Atlantic. Geography # It stretches about 3,800 km from Gibraltar to the Levant and is divided by Sicily and Tunisia into western and eastern basins, with sub-seas including the Alboran, Balearic, Ligurian, Tyrrhenian, Adriatic, Ionian, Aegean and Levantine seas. It connects to the Black Sea through the Dardanelles and Bosporus and to the Red Sea through the Suez Canal (1869). Seafloor and geology # The seafloor is tectonically active where the African plate pushes under Europe, creating the volcanoes of Etna, Vesuvius, Stromboli and Santorini and the deep Hellenic Trench, whose Calypso Deep (~5,267 m) is the sea’s deepest point. About 5.96–5.33 million years ago the Strait of Gibraltar closed and the sea nearly dried out (the Messinian salinity crisis), leaving salt layers over a kilometre thick; it refilled in the Zanclean flood. Water and currents # Atlantic surface water flows in at Gibraltar while dense, salty Mediterranean water (about 38–39 PSU) sinks and flows out beneath it, spreading through the Atlantic at around 1,000 m depth. Surface waters have warmed by more than 1 °C since the 1980s, and marine heatwaves pushed summer temperatures near 30 °C in 2022–2024. Climate, weather and cyclones # A hot, dry-summer ‘Mediterranean climate’. It is warming ~20% faster than the global ocean, with repeated marine heatwaves since 2003 causing mass die-offs of gorgonians and the noble pen shell. ‘Medicanes’ (Mediterranean hurricane-like storms) such as Daniel in 2023 caused catastrophic floods in Libya. Flora and fauna # Despite covering under 1% of the ocean, it holds roughly 7–10% of known marine species, including the Mediterranean monk seal, loggerhead and green turtles, fin and sperm whales, bluefin tuna, and the endemic seagrass Posidonia oceanica, whose meadows can be thousands of years old. Ecosystems # Posidonia seagrass meadows, coralligenous reefs of encrusting red algae, deep cold-water coral mounds, and lagoons such as the Venice lagoon. More than 1,000 non-native species, many arriving through the Suez Canal (‘Lessepsian migrants’) such as lionfish and rabbitfish, are reshaping the eastern basin. History and exploration # The cradle of Western seafaring: Minoan, Phoenician, Greek and Roman fleets; the Antikythera mechanism shipwreck; the battles of Salamis, Actium and Lepanto; Venetian and Genoese trade empires. Shipwrecks litter its floor from the Bronze Age Uluburun wreck onward. People and economy # About 150 million people live on its coasts and over 300 million tourists visit each year. Fisheries,

d: A tropical sea of coral reefs and the deepest point of the Caribbean, the Cayman Trough.
x: Overview # A tropical sea of about 2.75 million km² bounded by the Antilles island arcs, Central America and northern South America. It is famous for coral reefs, clear blue water and hurricanes, and for being the first region of the Americas reached by Columbus in 1492. Geography # It lies on the Caribbean plate, framed by the Greater Antilles (Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica, Puerto Rico) to the north and the Lesser Antilles volcanic arc to the east. It connects to the Gulf of Mexico through the Yucatán Channel and to the Pacific via the Panama Canal. Seafloor and geology # Its deepest point is the Cayman Trough (~7,686 m), where an ultra-slow spreading centre hosts the world’s deepest known hydrothermal vents (Beebe vent field, ~5,000 m). The Puerto Rico Trench just to the north is the deepest point of the Atlantic. Water and currents # Warm (26–29 °C), clear and low in nutrients. The Caribbean Current carries water westward into the Gulf of Mexico, where it becomes the Loop Current and feeds the Gulf Stream. Climate, weather and cyclones # The core of the Atlantic hurricane belt: warm water (>26.5°C) fuels storms from June to November. Sargassum influxes since 2011 smother beaches. Repeated heatwaves have bleached most reefs. Flora and fauna # Home to the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef (the second-largest barrier reef), staghorn and elkhorn corals, parrotfish, groupers, manatees, hawksbill and green turtles, and the vast seasonal mats of drifting Sargassum seaweed. Ecosystems # Fringing and barrier reefs, mangrove forests, seagrass beds, blue holes (such as Belize’s Great Blue Hole) and deep-sea vents. Many reefs have lost over half their coral cover since the 1970s. History and exploration # Indigenous Taíno and Kalinago peoples lived on the islands before European conquest. The sea became the centre of the plantation economy and the transatlantic slave trade, and the age of pirates; wrecks of Spanish treasure galleons still lie on its floor. People and economy # Tourism is the main industry for many island nations, alongside fishing and shipping through the Panama Canal. Threats and protection # Coral bleaching (mass events in 2005, 2010, 2023), stony coral tissue loss disease, invasive lionfish, overfishing, Sargassum influxes and stronger hurricanes.

d: A basin of natural oil seeps, brine pools and a large seasonal 'dead zone'.
x: Overview # An ocean basin of about 1.6 million km² enclosed by the USA, Mexico and Cuba. It is one of the world’s main oil and gas regions and a major fishery, and the birthplace of many Atlantic hurricanes’ most intense phases. Geography # Bounded by the US Gulf Coast, Mexico’s coast and the Yucatán Peninsula, and connected to the Atlantic through the Florida Straits and to the Caribbean through the Yucatán Channel. Seafloor and geology # Broad continental shelves surround a central abyssal plain reaching about 4,384 m in the Sigsbee Deep. Thick salt layers deposited ~160 million years ago form domes and trap oil. The Chicxulub crater, left by the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs, lies partly beneath its southern margin. Water and currents # The Loop Current carries warm Caribbean water through the Gulf before exiting as the Florida Current, the start of the Gulf Stream. The Mississippi River pours in nutrient-rich freshwater. Climate, weather and cyclones # The Loop Current feeds warm water that intensifies hurricanes (Katrina 2005, Harvey 2017, Ian 2022). Mississippi River nutrients create a summer ‘dead zone’ of hypoxic water averaging ~14,000 km². Flora and fauna # Bottlenose dolphins, sperm whales, whale sharks, Kemp’s ridley turtles (the most endangered sea turtle, nesting in Tamaulipas), red snapper, shrimp, oysters and Rice’s whale, a critically endangered species described in 2021. Ecosystems # Seagrass, oyster reefs, the Flower Garden Banks coral reefs, cold seeps with tubeworms and ice worms, and Kemp’s ridley turtle nesting beaches. History and exploration # Spanish explorers mapped it in the 16th century; it became the gateway for cotton and sugar exports via New Orleans. Hundreds of shipwrecks, including WWII U-boat victims, lie on its floor. People and economy # Produces about 15% of US crude oil and supports large shrimp, oyster and menhaden fisheries. Threats and protection # A seasonal ‘dead zone’ of low oxygen (often 10,000–20,000 km²) forms off Louisiana from Mississippi fertiliser runoff. The 2010 Deepwater Horizon blowout spilled about 4.9 million barrels of oil. Coastal Louisiana loses wetlands to subsidence and sea-level rise.

d: The only sea without coastlines, defined by currents and floating Sargassum seaweed.
x: Overview # The only sea without a coastline, defined by ocean currents rather than land. It lies in the North Atlantic subtropical gyre and is named after Sargassum, the golden-brown seaweed that floats in vast mats on its surface. Geography # Bounded by the Gulf Stream to the west, the North Atlantic Current to the north, the Canary Current to the east and the North Atlantic Equatorial Current to the south. Bermuda lies on its western edge. Seafloor and geology # Overlies deep abyssal plains (Nares and Hatteras) and the Bermuda Rise; about 4,500–6,500 m deep. Water and currents # Exceptionally clear, deep-blue, warm and nutrient-poor, with very little plankton. Being at the centre of a gyre, it gathers floating debris, part of the North Atlantic garbage patch. Climate, weather and cyclones # Bounded only by currents of the North Atlantic Gyre, so it has calm, clear, nutrient-poor warm water. The Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study (since 1988) records ocean warming and acidification here. Flora and fauna # Sargassum mats shelter a unique community: the Sargassum fish, Sargassum shrimp and crabs, juvenile sea turtles and baby fish. European and American eels migrate thousands of kilometres to spawn here, a mystery first solved by Johannes Schmidt in the 1920s. Ecosystems # Floating sargassum mats host endemic sargassum fish, crabs and nudibranchs, and nurseries for sea turtles. It is the spawning ground of European and American eels. History and exploration # Named by Portuguese sailors; Columbus feared his ships would be trapped in its weed. The 2014 Hamilton Declaration created a commission for its conservation. People and economy # Little direct use; it is a key area for long-term ocean monitoring at the Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study (BATS), running since 1988. Threats and protection # Plastic accumulation, shipping, and loss of eels whose numbers have collapsed by over 90% in some rivers. The Hamilton Declaration (2014) set up an international commission to protect it.

d: A shallow, heavily used shelf sea between Britain and mainland Europe.
x: Overview # A shallow shelf sea of about 575,000 km² between Britain, Scandinavia, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. It is one of the busiest seas on Earth for shipping, fishing, oil, gas and wind power. Geography # Connected to the Atlantic in the north and through the English Channel in the south, and to the Baltic through the Skagerrak and Kattegat. Seafloor and geology # A shallow shelf sea (average ~95 m) that was dry land, Doggerland, until about 8,000 years ago; fishermen still trawl up mammoth bones and Stone Age tools. The Norwegian Trench reaches ~700 m. Water and currents # Cool, well mixed by strong tides and storms, with lower salinity near river mouths such as the Rhine and Elbe. Climate, weather and cyclones # Severe winter storms and storm surges (the 1953 flood killed over 2,000 people in the Netherlands and UK). Warming has shifted cod north and brought in warm-water species. Flora and fauna # Atlantic cod, herring, mackerel, plaice, harbour porpoises, grey and harbour seals, and huge seabird colonies such as gannets at Bass Rock. Ecosystems # The Wadden Sea, a UNESCO site of tidal flats from the Netherlands to Denmark, is one of the largest intertidal systems in the world; sandbanks such as Dogger Bank. History and exploration # Viking routes, the Hanseatic League, the Battle of Jutland (1916) whose wrecks lie on the floor, North Sea oil since 1970 and now the world’s largest offshore wind farms. People and economy # North Sea oil and gas since the 1960s; today it is the world’s leading offshore-wind region. Ports include Rotterdam, Europe’s largest. Threats and protection # Past overfishing collapsed cod stocks; pollution, seabed trawling and the industrialisation of the sea with wind farms and cables.

d: A young brackish sea with some of the largest dead zones on Earth.
x: Overview # A young, shallow, brackish sea of about 377,000 km² enclosed by nine countries. It is one of the largest bodies of brackish water in the world, with a mix of marine and freshwater species. Geography # Bordered by Sweden, Finland, Russia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Germany and Denmark; it includes the Gulfs of Bothnia, Finland and Riga and connects to the North Sea through the Danish straits. Seafloor and geology # Average depth only about 55 m, with a deepest point of 459 m (Landsort Deep). It formed as ice sheets melted after the last Ice Age, and parts of Scandinavia are still rising from post-glacial rebound. Water and currents # Salinity falls from about 20 PSU near Denmark to almost fresh in the northern Gulf of Bothnia. A permanent salinity layer limits mixing, so deep water depends on rare inflows of salty North Sea water. Climate, weather and cyclones # Very low salinity (from ~2 PSU in the north to ~20 at the entrance) and limited exchange with the North Sea make it vulnerable. Its deep basins have one of the world’s largest dead zones, caused by nutrient runoff. Flora and fauna # Baltic herring, cod, sprat, ringed and grey seals, harbour porpoises (the Baltic Proper population is critically endangered), and bladderwrack forests. Ecosystems # A mix of marine and freshwater species, bladderwrack, grey and ringed seals, harbour porpoises, cod and herring. History and exploration # The Hanseatic trading league, Swedish and Russian empires, and the 1628 Vasa warship, raised almost intact because the brackish water lacks shipworms. Countless wrecks are preserved. People and economy # Shipping, ferries, fishing and gas pipelines; the Nord Stream pipelines were sabotaged in 2022. Threats and protection # Has some of the world’s largest dead zones (up to ~70,000 km²) from fertiliser runoff; dumped WWII chemical munitions; cod stocks collapsed and fishing for eastern Baltic cod was closed in 2019.

d: The largest anoxic body of water on Earth: below ~150–200 m there is no oxygen.
x: Overview # An inland sea of about 436,000 km² between Europe and Asia. Below about 150–200 m its water contains no oxygen and is full of hydrogen sulphide, making it the world’s largest anoxic water body. Geography # Bordered by Ukraine, Russia, Georgia, Turkey, Bulgaria and Romania; connected to the Mediterranean through the Bosporus and Dardanelles, and to the Sea of Azov. The Danube, Dnieper and Don pour in fresh water. Seafloor and geology # A deep basin (~2,212 m) linked to the Mediterranean only by the narrow Bosporus. Below ~150 m the water has no oxygen and is full of hydrogen sulfide, the largest anoxic water body on Earth. Water and currents # A low-salinity surface layer (about 18 PSU) sits on dense saltier water; this layering prevents oxygen from reaching the depths, so about 90% of its volume is anoxic. Climate, weather and cyclones # Strong stratification: a fresher surface layer from rivers (Danube, Dnieper, Don) sits above dense salty water that never mixes. Flora and fauna # Black Sea bottlenose dolphins, harbour porpoises, anchovy (hamsi), turbot, sturgeons (critically endangered) and the invasive comb jelly Mnemiopsis that crashed fisheries in the 1980s. Ecosystems # Surface life includes dolphins, anchovy and turbot; the sulfidic depths hold only microbes. The invasive comb jelly Mnemiopsis collapsed fisheries in the 1980s. History and exploration # Greek colonies, the Byzantine and Ottoman empires and Crimean wars. In 2018 researchers found a 2,400-year-old Greek merchant ship, the oldest intact shipwreck known, perfectly preserved without oxygen. People and economy # Fishing, ports such as Odesa and Constanța, grain exports and tourism. Threats and protection # Pollution, invasive species, overfishing and the effects of war, including dam destruction (Kakhovka, 2023) and mines.

d: A young ocean in the making, with heat-tolerant corals and hot brine pools.
x: Overview # A narrow, very salty sea of about 438,000 km² between Africa and Arabia, formed as the two continents split apart. It is famous for some of the world’s most heat-tolerant coral reefs. Geography # Runs about 2,250 km from the Gulf of Suez and Gulf of Aqaba to the Bab-el-Mandeb strait and the Gulf of Aden; bordered by Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Jordan and Israel. Seafloor and geology # A young ocean in the making: a spreading rift down its centre reaches about 3,040 m, with hot, salty brine pools on the seafloor that are toxic to most life. Water and currents # One of the saltiest seas (about 40 PSU) because of intense evaporation and no rivers, and very warm (surface often 26–32 °C). Climate, weather and cyclones # Among the warmest and saltiest seas (~40 PSU) because of extreme evaporation and almost no rivers. Its northern corals are unusually heat-tolerant and may be a refuge as oceans warm. Flora and fauna # Over 1,200 fish species (about 10% found nowhere else), dugongs, spinner dolphins, sharks and around 300 species of hard coral. Ecosystems # Northern Red Sea corals in the Gulf of Aqaba tolerate heat that bleaches corals elsewhere, possibly making them a refuge for reefs under warming. History and exploration # Ancient Egyptian expeditions to Punt, Roman trade with India, and the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869. People and economy # About 12% of global trade passed through it before 2024; attacks on shipping by Houthi forces from late 2023 diverted many ships around Africa. Threats and protection # Coastal development, tourism, shipping accidents, and the decaying FSO Safer oil tanker, whose oil was transferred in 2023 to avert a disaster.

d: Home to one of the world's thickest oxygen minimum zones, driven by monsoon upwelling.
x: Overview # The northwestern part of the Indian Ocean, about 3.86 million km², between India, Pakistan, Iran, Oman and the Horn of Africa. It is one of the most biologically productive seas, driven by monsoon upwelling. Geography # Includes the Gulf of Aden, Gulf of Oman and Laccadive Sea, with the Lakshadweep and Maldive islands to the southeast. Major ports include Mumbai, Karachi, Kochi and Muscat. Seafloor and geology # Deepest about 4,652 m; the Carlsberg Ridge spreads apart in the southwest, and the Indus Fan, one of the largest sediment fans in the world, spreads from the Indus delta. Water and currents # In summer the southwest monsoon drives strong upwelling off Oman and Somalia, bringing up nutrients. Below the surface lies one of the world’s largest oxygen minimum zones. Climate, weather and cyclones # The southwest monsoon drives intense upwelling and plankton blooms. It holds one of the world’s thickest oxygen minimum zones, and cyclones have become more frequent as it warms (e.g. Tauktae 2021 and Biparjoy 2023). Flora and fauna # Blue whales (a resident, non-migratory population), dolphins, sardines and mackerel that support Kerala’s fisheries, whale sharks off Gujarat, and the Arabian humpback whale, the most isolated humpback population. Ecosystems # Upwelling-driven fisheries (oil sardine, mackerel), Lakshadweep atolls and the Gulf of Kutch coral reefs. History and exploration # Monsoon sailing linked India, Arabia, Persia and East Africa for over 2,000 years; ports like Muziris, Calicut and Surat drew traders from Rome to Portugal. People and economy # Fisheries, oil tankers from the Persian Gulf, and the ports of Mumbai and Karachi. Threats and protection # Expanding oxygen-poor zones, warming, cyclones, overfishing and plastic.

d: The world's largest bay, freshened by the Ganges–Brahmaputra and fuelling strong cyclones.
x: Overview # The largest bay in the world, about 2.17 million km², bordered by India, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. Fed by the Ganges, Brahmaputra and other great rivers, it is one of the world’s most cyclone-prone and densely populated coasts. Geography # Its coasts include Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal; the Andaman and Nicobar Islands mark its eastern edge. Seafloor and geology # Covered by the Bengal Fan, the largest submarine fan on Earth, built from Himalayan sediment and up to 16 km thick in places. The Swatch of No Ground canyon cuts into the shelf. Water and currents # Enormous river discharge makes its surface water relatively fresh and layered, keeping the surface warm and helping fuel cyclones. Climate, weather and cyclones # Has produced many of history’s deadliest cyclones, including the 1970 Bhola cyclone (around 300,000–500,000 deaths), the 1999 Odisha super cyclone, Amphan (2020) and Fani (2019). Better warnings have cut death tolls dramatically. Flora and fauna # Olive ridley turtles nesting in mass arribadas at Gahirmatha and Rushikulya, Irrawaddy dolphins, Bryde’s whales, hilsa fish and the Sundarbans tiger. Ecosystems # The Sundarbans mangroves, olive ridley mass-nesting in Odisha, hilsa runs, Irrawaddy dolphins and the Andaman reefs. History and exploration # The Chola navy, Kalinga traders to Southeast Asia, and colonial ports of Calcutta, Madras and Chittagong. People and economy # Supports millions of fishers, ports and ship-breaking at Chittagong. Threats and protection # Sea-level rise and storm surges, an expanding oxygen-poor zone, plastic and overfishing.

d: Home to the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system on Earth.
x: Overview # A tropical sea of about 4.8 million km² off northeastern Australia, home to the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system on Earth. Geography # Bounded by Queensland, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia. Seafloor and geology # Includes the Queensland Plateau and deep basins over 9,000 m in the New Hebrides Trench region; many reefs sit on submerged plateaus. Water and currents # Warm and clear, driven by the East Australian Current. Climate, weather and cyclones # Cyclone-prone in the austral summer; repeated mass bleaching since 1998 (2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024). Flora and fauna # About 1,500 fish species on the Great Barrier Reef, dugongs, green and loggerhead turtles, humpback and dwarf minke whales, and over 400 hard coral species. Ecosystems # The Great Barrier Reef, the world’s largest reef system, with ~1,500 fish species, dugongs, nesting turtles and Osprey Reef sharks. History and exploration # Site of the 1942 Battle of the Coral Sea, the first naval battle fought entirely by aircraft carriers, which halted Japan’s advance toward Australia. People and economy # Reef tourism and fisheries worth billions to Australia. Threats and protection # Mass coral bleaching (2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024), crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks, farm runoff and cyclones.

d: A biodiverse and contested sea crossed by a large share of global shipping.
x: Overview # A marginal sea of about 3.5 million km² in the western Pacific, rich in reefs, fisheries and possible oil and gas. It carries roughly a third of global maritime trade and is the scene of overlapping territorial claims. Geography # Bordered by China, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei, Indonesia and Vietnam, and containing the Spratly and Paracel islands and Scarborough Shoal. Seafloor and geology # Its central basin reaches about 5,016 m; it opened by seafloor spreading between ~32 and 16 million years ago. Water and currents # Monsoon winds reverse surface currents seasonally; the Kuroshio intrudes through the Luzon Strait. Climate, weather and cyclones # Typhoon-prone; driven by the East Asian monsoon. Flora and fauna # About a third of the world’s marine biodiversity by some estimates, giant clams, dugongs, green turtles and many reef fish. Ecosystems # Coral reefs at the edge of the Coral Triangle, seagrass, and some of the world’s most heavily fished waters. History and exploration # Maritime Silk Road trade; today about a third of global shipping passes through, and overlapping territorial claims make it a geopolitical flashpoint. People and economy # Fisheries employing millions and shipping through the Strait of Malacca. Threats and protection # Island-building that destroyed reefs, giant-clam poaching, overfishing and maritime confrontations.

d: A semi-enclosed sea that forms its own deep water, like a mini-ocean.
x: Overview # A marginal sea of about 978,000 km² between Japan, Korea and Russia, called the East Sea in Korea. It is almost enclosed, connected to other seas by shallow straits. Geography # Bounded by Honshu and Hokkaido, the Korean Peninsula and the Russian Far East, with the Tsushima, Tsugaru, La Pérouse and Tatar straits. Seafloor and geology # Deep basins reach about 3,742 m; the sea opened as Japan split from the Asian mainland ~20–15 million years ago. Water and currents # Has its own cold, oxygen-rich deep water formed in winter off Vladivostok; the warm Tsushima Current flows in from the south. Climate, weather and cyclones # Cold winter monsoon winds form deep water locally; this formation has weakened with warming. Flora and fauna # Snow crabs, squid, Pacific saury, salmon, spotted seals and Steller sea lions. Ecosystems # Snow crabs, firefly squid (Toyama Bay), Japanese flying squid and Pacific saury. History and exploration # The 1905 Battle of Tsushima. The sea’s name is disputed (Korea uses ‘East Sea’). People and economy # Fisheries and shipping between Japan, Korea, China and Russia. Threats and protection # Warming faster than the global average, declining deep-water oxygen and overfishing.

d: One of the most productive seas on Earth, supporting huge pollock and crab fisheries.
x: Overview # A cold, highly productive sea of about 2 million km² between Alaska and Russia’s Kamchatka and Chukotka. It supplies around 40% of the US seafood catch. Geography # Bounded by the Aleutian Islands to the south and the Bering Strait, just 82 km wide, to the north. Seafloor and geology # A wide continental shelf in the northeast and the deep Aleutian Basin (about 4,000 m) in the southwest. In the Ice Age the shelf was dry land, Beringia, across which people reached the Americas. Water and currents # Sea ice forms in winter and melts in spring, fuelling huge plankton blooms. Climate, weather and cyclones # Seasonal sea ice drives the ecosystem; the 2018–19 ice-free winters and heatwave triggered the collapse of the snow crab fishery. Flora and fauna # Walruses, Steller sea lions, northern fur seals, gray and bowhead whales, king and snow crabs, pollock and salmon. Ecosystems # Walrus, Steller sea lions, northern fur seals, seabirds in millions, and the pollock and king crab fisheries. History and exploration # Vitus Bering’s expeditions (1728, 1741); Russian America and the 1867 Alaska purchase. People and economy # The Alaska pollock fishery, among the world’s largest; Indigenous Yup’ik and Iñupiat communities. Threats and protection # Loss of sea ice; the snow crab population crashed after a 2018–2019 heatwave, closing the fishery in 2022–23.

d: A major source of Antarctic Bottom Water and the resting place of Shackleton's Endurance.
x: Overview # A large sea of the Southern Ocean east of the Antarctic Peninsula, partly covered by the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf. It produces much of the cold, dense Antarctic Bottom Water that spreads through the world’s ocean. Geography # Between the Antarctic Peninsula and Coats Land. Seafloor and geology # Deep shelf and abyssal plain; the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf covers its southern part. Water and currents # Among the clearest seawater ever measured; brine from freezing sea ice sinks to form bottom water. Climate, weather and cyclones # The main source of Antarctic Bottom Water. Its clockwise gyre traps thick sea ice. Flora and fauna # Emperor penguins, Weddell seals, crabeater seals, krill and the world’s largest known fish breeding colony (about 60 million icefish nests found in 2021). Ecosystems # Emperor penguin colonies, Weddell seals and, in 2021, a vast colony of ~60 million nesting icefish found on the seabed. History and exploration # Shackleton’s Endurance was crushed by ice here in 1915; its wreck was found in 2022 at about 3,008 m. People and economy # Scientific stations; proposed as a marine protected area. Threats and protection # Warming and sea-ice change; krill fishing.

d: Often called the most pristine marine ecosystem left, and protected by a large MPA since 2017.
x: Overview # A deep bay of the Southern Ocean, often called the last largely intact marine ecosystem on Earth. It hosts the world’s largest marine protected area (1.55 million km², established 2017). Geography # Bounded by the Ross Ice Shelf, the largest ice shelf in Antarctica, and Victoria Land. Seafloor and geology # Contains the Ross Ice Shelf, the largest floating ice shelf (about the size of France). Water and currents # Very cold, nutrient-rich water and huge polynyas (open-water areas within the ice). Climate, weather and cyclones # Polynyas produce sea ice and dense water; considered one of the least altered ocean ecosystems. Flora and fauna # Antarctic toothfish, Adélie and emperor penguins, Weddell seals, orcas and minke whales. Ecosystems # Antarctic toothfish, Adélie and emperor penguins, Ross Sea orcas and Weddell seals. History and exploration # Ross discovered it in 1841. The Ross Sea MPA (2016) was the first large high-seas MPA, about 1.55 million km². People and economy # Science and limited toothfish fishing outside the protected area. Threats and protection # Toothfish fishing pressure, warming.

d: A hot, hyper-saline shallow sea whose corals survive extremes that kill corals elsewhere.
x: Overview # A shallow, very warm and salty sea of about 251,000 km² between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, holding some of the world’s largest oil and gas reserves. Geography # Bordered by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar and the UAE; connected to the Gulf of Oman through the Strait of Hormuz. Seafloor and geology # Shallow (average ~35 m), formed as a foreland basin of the Zagros mountains; dry land during the last ice age. Water and currents # Summer surface temperatures exceed 34 °C, some of the hottest seawater on Earth, and salinity tops 40 PSU. Climate, weather and cyclones # Some of the hottest seawater on Earth (over 35°C in summer) and very salty; its corals tolerate heat that would kill others. Flora and fauna # Its corals survive extreme heat; it supports dugongs (one of the largest populations outside Australia), green turtles and pearl oysters. Ecosystems # Corals, dugongs, seagrass and pearl oysters. History and exploration # A pearling centre for millennia; the 1991 Gulf War spill was one of the largest oil spills ever. People and economy # Oil, gas and around a fifth of the world’s oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz; desalination plants supply drinking water. Threats and protection # Brine discharge, heat-driven coral bleaching, coastal reclamation and oil pollution.

d: Between Australia and New Zealand, a marine-heatwave hotspot.
x: Overview # The sea between Australia and New Zealand, about 2,300 km wide, famous for rough seas and the warm East Australian Current. Geography # Bounded by southeastern Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand, with Lord Howe Island in its north. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 5,943 m; the sea opened 85–52 million years ago as Zealandia separated from Australia. Water and currents # The East Australian Current is strengthening and warming, making this one of the fastest-warming ocean regions. Climate, weather and cyclones # The East Australian Current is warming it rapidly, making it a marine heatwave hotspot. Flora and fauna # Southern right whales, fur seals, great white sharks, albatrosses and kelp forests. Ecosystems # Lord Howe Island’s southernmost coral reef and Tasmanian giant kelp forests (over 95% lost since the 1940s). History and exploration # Named after Abel Tasman (1642). People and economy # Fishing and shipping between Australia and New Zealand. Threats and protection # Marine heatwaves and loss of giant kelp.

d: A huge inland sea where polar bears depend on seasonal ice.
x: Overview # A vast inland sea of about 1.23 million km² in northern Canada, frozen for much of the year. Geography # Bordered by Nunavut, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec; connected to the Atlantic through Hudson Strait. Seafloor and geology # Shallow (average about 100 m); the land around it is still rising after the weight of the Ice Age ice sheet was removed. Water and currents # Low salinity from many rivers; ice-free only from about July to October. Climate, weather and cyclones # Ice-covered most of the year; ice-free seasons lengthening, stressing polar bears. Flora and fauna # Polar bears that hunt seals on the sea ice, belugas (tens of thousands gather in the Churchill estuary), walruses and narwhals. Ecosystems # Polar bears around Churchill, beluga whales in summer estuaries, and ringed seals. History and exploration # The Hudson’s Bay Company (1670) controlled the fur trade across a vast area. People and economy # Inuit and Cree communities; the port of Churchill. Threats and protection # Earlier ice break-up is shortening polar bears’ hunting season and their numbers are falling.

d: The Arctic's 'hot spot' of warming, where Atlantic water is pushing north.
x: Overview # An Arctic shelf sea of about 1.4 million km² north of Norway and Russia, kept partly ice-free by Atlantic water. Geography # Bounded by Svalbard, Franz Josef Land and Novaya Zemlya. Seafloor and geology # A broad shelf sea (average ~230 m) warmed by Atlantic water. Water and currents # Warm Atlantic water enters from the southwest; it is warming so fast that scientists describe its ‘Atlantification’. Climate, weather and cyclones # Rapid ‘Atlantification’: sea ice retreating and Atlantic species moving in. Flora and fauna # The world’s largest cod stock (northeast Arctic cod), capelin, herring, walruses, polar bears and red king crab (introduced by the Soviets in the 1960s). Ecosystems # Among the largest cod stocks, capelin, and introduced red king crabs. History and exploration # Willem Barentsz explored it in 1596; it was a WWII Arctic convoy route. People and economy # Rich fisheries and gas fields. Threats and protection # Rapid sea-ice loss, warming and nuclear waste dumped by the Soviet Union.

d: The largest enclosed inland body of water, salty but not connected to the ocean.
x: Overview # The largest enclosed inland body of water on Earth (about 371,000 km²), technically a lake but salty like a sea. It is shrinking. Geography # Bordered by Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan; fed mainly by the Volga. Seafloor and geology # Shallow north (a few metres) and deep south (about 1,025 m). Its surface lies about 28 m below sea level. Water and currents # Salinity about 12 PSU, about a third of the ocean’s. Climate, weather and cyclones # Water level fluctuates with Volga inflow and is now falling due to evaporation and warming. Flora and fauna # About 90% of the world’s wild caviar-producing sturgeon (now critically endangered) and the Caspian seal. Ecosystems # The Volga delta and coastal wetlands. History and exploration # Ancient trade routes and Baku’s oil boom in the 19th century. People and economy # Oil and gas, fishing. Threats and protection # Falling water levels, which could drop by 9–18 m this century; overfishing of sturgeon; pollution.

d: A tropical sea between Myanmar, Thailand and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
x: Overview # A tropical sea of about 600,000 km² in the northeastern Indian Ocean, between Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia and India’s Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Geography # Bounded by the Andaman and Nicobar ridge on the west and the Malay Peninsula on the east; connects to the Strait of Malacca. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 4,198 m; an active back-arc basin with a spreading ridge and Barren Island, India’s only active volcano. Water and currents # Monsoon-driven circulation and large internal waves visible from space. Climate, weather and cyclones # Hit by the 2004 tsunami; cyclones form in spring and autumn. Flora and fauna # Reef fish, manta rays, dugongs, leatherback turtles nesting in the Nicobars and saltwater crocodiles. Ecosystems # Coral reefs (Similan and Surin islands, Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park), mangroves and seagrass. History and exploration # The 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake (magnitude 9.1) caused the Indian Ocean tsunami. People and economy # Tourism (Phuket, Havelock/Swaraj Dweep) and fishing. Threats and protection # Coral bleaching, overfishing and development.

d: The sea bordering southwest India, Sri Lanka and the Maldives, containing the Lakshadweep islands.
x: Overview # A warm sea off southwestern India and the Maldives, also known as the Lakshadweep Sea, rich in coral atolls. Geography # Bounded by Kerala, Sri Lanka, the Lakshadweep islands and the Maldives. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 4,131 m; the atolls sit on the Chagos–Laccadive Ridge, a volcanic track. Water and currents # Warm water (26–30 °C) with seasonal upwelling off Kerala. Climate, weather and cyclones # Southwest monsoon arrives here first, usually around 1 June over Kerala. Flora and fauna # Coral reef fish, tuna, sea turtles, dolphins and the oil sardine that sustains Kerala’s fishers. Ecosystems # Atolls, lagoons and seagrass beds. History and exploration # Arab and Indian traders sailed it for centuries; Lakshadweep’s people are mostly Muslim seafarers. People and economy # Fisheries, coconut and growing tourism. Threats and protection # Bleaching in 1998, 2010, 2016 and 2024; sea-level rise for atolls.

d: A shallow gulf between India and Sri Lanka, home to India's first marine biosphere reserve.
x: Overview # A shallow inlet of the Indian Ocean between southeastern India and Sri Lanka, and one of the richest marine areas in South Asia. Its 21 islands form India’s first marine biosphere reserve (1989). Geography # Lies south of Rameswaram and Ram Setu (Adam’s Bridge), a chain of shoals linking India and Sri Lanka. Seafloor and geology # Mostly shallow coral and sand; deeper to the south. Water and currents # Warm and clear, with seasonal currents. Climate, weather and cyclones # Northeast monsoon rains in October–December. Flora and fauna # Dugongs (one of India’s last strongholds), sea turtles, dolphins, over 100 coral species, sea cucumbers and pearl oysters. Ecosystems # Coral reefs fringing the islands, seagrass meadows that feed dugongs, and mangroves. History and exploration # Famous since antiquity for pearl fisheries mentioned by Pliny and Marco Polo. People and economy # Fishing communities, chank (conch) shell collection and seaweed farming. Threats and protection # Coral mining (now banned), bottom trawling, bleaching and sea-level rise.

d: The southernmost sea that freezes regularly, bordering Russia and Hokkaido.
x: Overview # A cold marginal sea of about 1.6 million km² enclosed by Siberia, Kamchatka, the Kuril Islands and Hokkaido. It has the southernmost seasonal sea ice in the Northern Hemisphere. Geography # Bounded by the Russian mainland, Sakhalin, Kamchatka and the Kuril chain. Seafloor and geology # Shelves in the north and the Kuril Basin (about 3,372 m) in the south. Water and currents # Sea ice forms each winter, producing dense water that ventilates the intermediate North Pacific. Climate, weather and cyclones # Drift ice reaches Hokkaido, the world’s lowest-latitude seasonal sea ice. Flora and fauna # Pollock, salmon, king crab, Steller sea lions, spotted seals, bowhead and right whales. Ecosystems # Sea-ice-edge plankton blooms and drift ice off Hokkaido’s Shiretoko (UNESCO). History and exploration # Russian expansion to the Pacific from the 17th century. People and economy # Pollock, crab and salmon fisheries; Sakhalin oil. Threats and protection # Declining sea ice and oil development.

d: A broad shelf sea fed by the Yangtze, the largest river in Asia.
x: Overview # A marginal sea of about 1.25 million km² between China, Korea, Japan and Taiwan, fed by the Yangtze, Asia’s longest river. Geography # Wide continental shelf and the Okinawa Trough, with hydrothermal vents. Seafloor and geology # Wide continental shelf; the Okinawa Trough reaches about 2,716 m and has hydrothermal vents. Water and currents # The warm Kuroshio Current flows along its eastern edge; Yangtze outflow lowers salinity. Climate, weather and cyclones # Vent fauna in the Okinawa Trough, Nomura’s jellyfish blooms, hairtail and yellow croaker. Flora and fauna # Hairtail, yellow croaker, squid and jellyfish blooms. Ecosystems # Estuarine and shelf ecosystems. History and exploration # Trade routes between China, Korea and Japan; disputes over the Senkaku/Diaoyu islands. People and economy # Huge fisheries and shipping through Shanghai, the world’s busiest container port. Threats and protection # Overfishing, pollution and a summer low-oxygen zone off the Yangtze.

d: A shallow sea between China and Korea, named for sediment from the Yellow River.
x: Overview # A shallow sea between China and Korea named for the yellow silt carried by the Yellow River. Geography # Includes the Bohai Sea; bordered by China and the Korean Peninsula. Seafloor and geology # Average depth only about 44 m; it was dry land in the Ice Age. Water and currents # Strong tides and a cold water mass in summer. Climate, weather and cyclones # Cold, dry winters and monsoon summers. Flora and fauna # Its tidal flats are a crucial stopover for migratory shorebirds such as the spoon-billed sandpiper and great knot. Ecosystems # Among the largest tidal mudflats on Earth (UNESCO World Heritage, 2019). History and exploration # Coastal trade, Korean War landings at Incheon. People and economy # Fisheries and land reclamation. Threats and protection # Reclamation destroyed much of the tidal flats; algal blooms.

d: A deep marginal sea east of the Philippines, bordered by the Mariana arc.
x: Overview # A vast sea of about 5 million km² east of the Philippines and Taiwan, bounded by island arcs and some of the deepest trenches on Earth. Geography # Bounded by the Philippines, Taiwan, Japan, the Marianas and Palau. Seafloor and geology # On its eastern edge is the Mariana Trench, with the Challenger Deep (~10,935 m), the deepest point on Earth; the Philippine Trench reaches about 10,540 m. Water and currents # Warm surface water; source of the Kuroshio Current. Climate, weather and cyclones # The most active typhoon nursery on Earth. Flora and fauna # Tuna, whales, deep-sea snailfish (filmed at 8,336 m in 2022) and coral reefs. Ecosystems # Island reefs and hadal trench communities. History and exploration # The 1944 Battle of the Philippine Sea, one of the largest carrier battles. People and economy # Fisheries and shipping lanes. Threats and protection # Warming, typhoon intensification.

d: A shallow equatorial sea in the heart of Indonesia.
x: Overview # A shallow, warm sea of about 320,000 km² between Java, Borneo and Sumatra. Geography # Part of the Sunda Shelf, which was dry land during the Ice Age. Seafloor and geology # Average depth about 46 m. Water and currents # Warm, low in salinity due to heavy rain. Climate, weather and cyclones # Equatorial; heavy rainfall. Flora and fauna # Coral reefs, sea turtles and important fisheries. Ecosystems # Karimunjawa reefs and mangroves. History and exploration # Battle of the Java Sea (1942); many WWII wrecks, some illegally salvaged. People and economy # Fishing and shipping; Jakarta is sinking and Indonesia is moving its capital to Nusantara. Threats and protection # Pollution, overfishing and coastal subsidence.

d: A deep sea in eastern Indonesia, home to the deepest forearc basin on Earth.
x: Overview # A deep sea in eastern Indonesia surrounded by islands and once the source of the world’s nutmeg and mace. Geography # Bounded by the Moluccas, Sulawesi, Timor and the Banda Islands. Seafloor and geology # The Weber Deep reaches about 7,200 m, the deepest point of any sea not in a trench system. Water and currents # Part of the Indonesian Throughflow, carrying Pacific water to the Indian Ocean. Climate, weather and cyclones # Monsoon climate. Flora and fauna # Hammerhead sharks, blue whales and rich reefs. Ecosystems # Volcanic island reefs. History and exploration # The Banda Islands were the only source of nutmeg; in 1621 the Dutch massacred most of the islanders to control the trade. People and economy # Fishing and spice farming. Threats and protection # Overfishing, warming.

d: A basin sea in the southwest Philippines holding Tubbataha Reef.
x: Overview # A sea between the Philippines and Malaysian Borneo, home to the Tubbataha Reefs, one of the best-protected reefs in Asia. Geography # Bounded by Palawan, Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago. Seafloor and geology # Deep basin surrounded by shallow sills. Water and currents # Warm and isolated from the Pacific’s deep water. Climate, weather and cyclones # Typhoons rarely reach it. Flora and fauna # Over 600 fish species at Tubbataha, sharks, turtles and manta rays. Ecosystems # Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park (UNESCO). History and exploration # The Sultanate of Sulu was a maritime trading power. People and economy # Fishing and seaweed farming. Threats and protection # Piracy and illegal fishing.

d: A deep sea in the Coral Triangle known for mysterious midwater animals.
x: Overview # A deep sea between the southern Philippines and Indonesia’s Sulawesi (Celebes). Geography # Bounded by Mindanao, Sulawesi and Borneo. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 6,200 m; formed as ancient ocean floor about 42 million years ago. Water and currents # Warm surface water; part of the Indonesian Throughflow. Climate, weather and cyclones # Equatorial. Flora and fauna # Whale sharks, turtles, tuna and the coelacanth’s Indonesian relative (Latimeria menadoensis) found off Sulawesi in 1998. Ecosystems # Coral reefs of the Coral Triangle. History and exploration # Maritime trade routes of the Bajau ‘sea nomads’. People and economy # Fisheries. Threats and protection # Overfishing and blast fishing.

d: The 'aquarium of the world', a young sea opening as Baja California splits from Mexico.
x: Overview # A narrow sea about 1,100 km long and 160,000 km² in area, separating the Baja California peninsula from mainland Mexico. Jacques Cousteau called it ‘the world’s aquarium’ for its astonishing density of life. It is a young sea, opened over the last 5–6 million years as Baja California has been torn away from the North American mainland. Geography # Bounded by Baja California (west) and the Mexican states of Sonora and Sinaloa (east). The Colorado River once poured into its northern end, but is now almost entirely diverted for irrigation. It contains over 900 islands and islets, including Tiburón, the largest island in Mexico. Seafloor and geology # An active rift: a chain of deep basins (Guaymas, Carmen, Farallón, Pescadero) where the East Pacific Rise spreading ridge links to the San Andreas Fault. Pescadero Basin hosts the deepest known hydrothermal vents in the Pacific (~3,700 m). Guaymas Basin vents bubble through thick sediment and grow oily microbial mats. Water and currents # Strong tides (up to ~7 m in the north) and wind-driven upwelling stir nutrients from the depths, feeding intense plankton blooms. The north is hotter and saltier because of evaporation and little fresh water. Climate, weather and cyclones # Desert climate on both shores, with very hot summers. Hurricanes from the eastern Pacific sometimes strike, such as Odile (2014). The North American monsoon brings summer storms. Flora and fauna # Around 900 fish species (about 90 endemic), about a third of the world’s marine mammal species including blue, fin, humpback and sperm whales, whale sharks, giant mobula ray aggregations that leap from the water, California sea lions and the endemic totoaba. It is the only home of the vaquita porpoise, the world’s rarest marine mammal, with probably fewer than about 10 left (surveys in 2023–2024 sighted 6–13). Ecosystems # Rocky reefs, mangroves, the Cabo Pulmo coral reef, a no-take zone where fish biomass rose by over 400% after protection, and the 244 islands and protected areas listed by UNESCO in 2005. History and exploration # Seri (Comcaac) and other Indigenous peoples fished it for millennia. Spanish explorers mapped it in the 16th century and believed Baja was an island. John Steinbeck and Ed Ricketts’ 1940 expedition produced The Log from the Sea of Cortez. People and economy # Shrimp trawling, sardine and squid fisheries, and growing tourism in Cabo San Lucas and La Paz. Threats and protection # Illegal gillnets set for the totoaba, whose swim bladder is smuggled to China, have driven the vaquita to the edge of extinction. Shrimp bycatch, the lost flow of the Colorado River delta and coastal development are other threats.

d: A shallow gulf bordered by Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.
x: Overview # A shallow gulf of about 320,000 km² in the South China Sea, bordered by Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia. Geography # Between the Malay Peninsula and Indochina. Seafloor and geology # Average depth about 45 m; dry land during the Ice Age. Water and currents # Warm and nutrient-rich. Climate, weather and cyclones # Monsoon rains; occasional typhoons. Flora and fauna # Irrawaddy dolphins, dugongs, whale sharks and reef fish. Ecosystems # Mangroves, seagrass and reefs around Ko Tao and Ko Chang. History and exploration # Trade routes of Ayutthaya and Funan. People and economy # Major fisheries, offshore gas and tourism. Threats and protection # Overfishing, mangrove loss for shrimp farms and bleaching.

d: A long arm of the Mediterranean between Italy and the Balkans.
x: Overview # An arm of the Mediterranean between Italy and the Balkans, about 800 km long. Geography # Bounded by Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Montenegro and Albania; Venice lies at its head. Seafloor and geology # Shallow in the north (under 100 m) and deeper in the south (about 1,233 m). Water and currents # The Po and other rivers lower salinity in the north; dense northern winter water spills southward. Climate, weather and cyclones # The cold bora wind and the warm sirocco, which drives Venice’s acqua alta floods. Flora and fauna # Over 1,000 Croatian islands, sea turtles, bottlenose dolphins. Ecosystems # Croatia’s 1,200 islands and karst coast. History and exploration # The Venetian Republic dominated it for centuries. People and economy # Tourism, fishing and ports; Venice’s MOSE flood barrier (2020). Threats and protection # Overfishing and nutrient pollution.

d: The island-studded sea between Greece and Turkey.
x: Overview # An arm of the Mediterranean between Greece and Turkey, scattered with about 1,400 islands. Geography # Includes the Cyclades, Dodecanese and Sporades; connects to the Black Sea through the Dardanelles. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 3,544 m; the Hellenic arc volcanoes include Santorini. Water and currents # Clear, warm in summer; Black Sea water flows in at the surface. Climate, weather and cyclones # Strong summer meltemi winds. Flora and fauna # Mediterranean monk seals, dolphins and Posidonia meadows. Ecosystems # Island reefs and seagrass. History and exploration # The cradle of Minoan and Greek civilisation; Santorini’s eruption around 1600 BCE; the Antikythera mechanism wreck. People and economy # Tourism, ferries and fishing. Threats and protection # Overfishing, tourism pressure and earthquakes.

d: A deep, volcanic part of the Mediterranean west of Italy.
x: Overview # A deep part of the western Mediterranean bounded by Italy, Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica. Geography # Includes the Bay of Naples and the Aeolian Islands. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 3,785 m with large underwater volcanoes such as Marsili, Europe’s biggest. Water and currents # Gyres and deep water. Climate, weather and cyclones # Mediterranean. Flora and fauna # Pelagos Sanctuary for whales in the north. Ecosystems # The Pelagos Sanctuary for whales (shared with the Ligurian Sea). History and exploration # Etruscan and Roman sea routes; Vesuvius buried Pompeii (79 CE). People and economy # Ports of Naples and Palermo and tourism. Threats and protection # Plastic hotspots (microplastics up to ~1.9 million particles per m² of seafloor).

d: A deep sea where warm Atlantic water cools, sinks and feeds the global overturning circulation.
x: Overview # A deep sea between Norway, Iceland and the Arctic, kept ice-free by the warm Norwegian Atlantic Current. Geography # Bounded by Norway, Iceland, Jan Mayen and the Greenland Sea. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 3,970 m; the Storegga Slide ~8,150 years ago caused a tsunami that hit Britain. Water and currents # A key part of the Atlantic overturning circulation. Climate, weather and cyclones # Mild for its latitude thanks to the Gulf Stream. Flora and fauna # Herring, mackerel, orcas and the world’s largest cold-water coral reef (Røst Reef). Ecosystems # Cold-water coral reefs and fjords. History and exploration # Viking voyages. People and economy # Fisheries, oil and gas, and salmon farming. Threats and protection # Warming and fish-farm pollution.

d: A key site where the North Atlantic overturns, forming deep water.
x: Overview # An arm of the North Atlantic between Labrador and Greenland where deep water forms in winter. Geography # Bounded by Canada’s Labrador coast and southwest Greenland. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 4,300 m. Water and currents # Winter cooling makes surface water sink, feeding the deep Atlantic. Climate, weather and cyclones # Icebergs from Greenland drift south (‘Iceberg Alley’). Flora and fauna # Harp seals, cod and seabirds. Ecosystems # Sea-ice and iceberg ecosystems. History and exploration # Vikings sailed past; the Titanic iceberg likely came via here. People and economy # Fisheries. Threats and protection # Freshening from Greenland melt may weaken deep-water formation.

d: A stormy sea between South America and Antarctica, rich in krill.
x: Overview # A stormy sea between South America and Antarctica, at the heart of the Antarctic krill fishery. Geography # Bounded by the Scotia Arc islands, including South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 8,264 m in the South Sandwich Trench. Water and currents # Antarctic Circumpolar Current through Drake Passage. Climate, weather and cyclones # Some of the roughest seas on Earth. Flora and fauna # Krill swarms feeding whales, seals and penguins; South Georgia wildlife. Ecosystems # Island ecosystems of South Georgia. History and exploration # Shackleton’s open-boat journey to South Georgia (1916). People and economy # Krill fishing. Threats and protection # Krill fishing pressure, warming.

d: The sea beside the Thwaites 'Doomsday' Glacier, where warm water melts ice from below.
x: Overview # A sea off West Antarctica where the fastest-melting glaciers, Thwaites and Pine Island, meet the ocean. Geography # Off Marie Byrd Land. Seafloor and geology # Deep glacial troughs channel warm water. Water and currents # Warm Circumpolar Deep Water melts ice shelves from below. Climate, weather and cyclones # Rapid ice-shelf thinning. Flora and fauna # Emperor penguins and seals. Ecosystems # Polynyas with intense blooms. History and exploration # Named after Roald Amundsen. People and economy # Research only. Threats and protection # Thwaites, the ‘Doomsday Glacier’, could add about 65 cm to sea level if it collapsed.

d: An Arctic sea north of Alaska and Canada, home to the Beaufort Gyre.
x: Overview # An Arctic sea north of Alaska and Canada. Geography # Bounded by Alaska’s North Slope and the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. Seafloor and geology # Shelf and the deep Canada Basin. Water and currents # The Beaufort Gyre stores Arctic freshwater. Climate, weather and cyclones # Sea ice most of the year, now melting further each summer. Flora and fauna # Bowhead whales, belugas, polar bears and ringed seals. Ecosystems # Sea-ice and coastal lagoons. History and exploration # Search for the Northwest Passage. People and economy # Iñupiat and Inuvialuit communities; oil fields at Prudhoe Bay. Threats and protection # Sea-ice loss and oil development.

d: A deep-water formation area between Greenland and Svalbard.
x: Overview # An Arctic sea between Greenland and Svalbard where cold East Greenland water meets Atlantic water. Geography # Between Greenland, Svalbard and Jan Mayen. Seafloor and geology # Reaches about 4,846 m. Water and currents # Deep-water formation feeds the Atlantic overturning circulation. Climate, weather and cyclones # Sea ice carried south by the East Greenland Current. Flora and fauna # Narwhals, walruses, hooded seals and polar bears. Ecosystems # Pack ice and polynyas. History and exploration # Whaling grounds from the 17th century. People and economy # Fisheries. Threats and protection # Warming and sea-ice loss.

d: A shallow sea between Ireland and Great Britain.
x: Overview # Separated by the North Channel and St George’s Channel. Geography # Includes Cardigan Bay and Liverpool Bay; the Isle of Man lies in the middle. Seafloor and geology # Shallow; dumped WWII munitions in Beaufort’s Dyke. Water and currents # Mixed by strong tides. Climate, weather and cyclones # Mild and stormy. Flora and fauna # Basking sharks, grey seals and harbour porpoises. Ecosystems # Sandbanks and estuaries. History and exploration # Viking raids; Liverpool’s port grew from Atlantic trade. People and economy # Ferries, wind farms and fishing. Threats and protection # Radioactive waste from Sellafield (historically) and overfishing.

d: A young rifting gulf linking the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
x: Overview # A deep gulf between Yemen and Somalia linking the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait. Geography # Bounded by Yemen, Djibouti and Somalia. Seafloor and geology # A young spreading ridge reaching about 5,390 m. Water and currents # Monsoon upwelling. Climate, weather and cyclones # Desert climate with monsoon winds. Flora and fauna # Sharks, dolphins and reefs. Ecosystems # Coral reefs off Socotra. History and exploration # Ancient incense and spice route; modern piracy hotspot.
