People and economy # A shipping lane carrying Suez traffic. Threats and protection # Piracy (peaked 2008–2011) and attacks on shipping since 2023.

d: The largest river by volume, carrying about a fifth of all river water that reaches the ocean.
x: Course and mouth # Rises in the Peruvian Andes and crosses Brazil to a mouth ~300 km wide; its freshwater plume extends hundreds of km into the Atlantic, and a reef system lies beneath it. Seasonal cycle and floods # Annual flood pulse raises water by 10–15 m, flooding forests (várzea and igapó) for months. Flora and fauna # Pink river dolphins, arapaima, piranhas, electric eels, Amazonian manatees, giant otters and over 3,000 fish species. People # Supports Indigenous peoples and cities like Manaus and Belém. Threats # Deforestation, dams, mercury from gold mining, drought (record lows 2023–24).

d: Often cited as the longest river, the lifeline of Egyptian civilisation.
x: Course and mouth # White Nile from Lake Victoria and Blue Nile from Ethiopia join at Khartoum, ending in a large delta. Seasonal cycle and floods # Historic summer flood from Ethiopian monsoon rains, now controlled by the Aswan High Dam (1970). Flora and fauna # Nile crocodiles, Nile perch, hippos, migratory birds on the delta. People # About 300 million people in 11 countries depend on it. Threats # Dams (including GERD), delta subsidence and saltwater intrusion.

d: Asia's longest river and home to the Three Gorges Dam.
x: Course and mouth # From the Tibetan Plateau to Shanghai. Seasonal cycle and floods # Summer monsoon floods. Flora and fauna # Yangtze finless porpoise, Chinese sturgeon; the baiji is functionally extinct. People # About 400 million people live in its basin. Threats # Dams, pollution, overfishing (10-year fishing ban from 2020).

d: North America's largest river system, draining ~40% of the contiguous USA.
x: Course and mouth # Ends in the bird’s-foot delta in Louisiana. Seasonal cycle and floods # Spring snowmelt and rain floods (1927, 1993). Flora and fauna # Paddlefish, alligator gar, catfish, migratory birds on the Mississippi Flyway. People # A key shipping corridor for grain. Threats # Nutrient runoff causing the Gulf dead zone; delta land loss.

d: The largest river flowing into the Arctic Ocean.
x: Course and mouth # From Mongolia through Siberia. Seasonal cycle and floods # Spring ice-breakup floods. Flora and fauna # Siberian sturgeon, taimen, Arctic char. People # Hydroelectric dams. Threats # Permafrost thaw, pollution.

d: Siberian river with one of the longest estuaries (Gulf of Ob).
x: Course and mouth # From the Altai mountains. Seasonal cycle and floods # Spring floods. Flora and fauna # Whitefish, sturgeon. People # Oil and gas region. Threats # Pollution, permafrost thaw.

d: Flows through permafrost to a vast Arctic delta.
x: Course and mouth # Delta is a protected wildlife reserve. Seasonal cycle and floods # Ice jams cause floods each spring. Flora and fauna # Migratory birds, Arctic fish. People # Yakutsk. Threats # Warming and erosion of permafrost banks.

d: The deepest river in the world (over 220 m) and second by discharge.
x: Course and mouth # Its submarine canyon carries sediment ~1,000 km out to sea. Seasonal cycle and floods # Crosses the equator twice, so it flows strongly year-round. Flora and fauna # Over 700 fish species, many endemic to rapids; bonobos on its banks. People # Kinshasa and Brazzaville. Threats # Deforestation, dams.

d: The world's largest inland fishery, flowing through six countries.
x: Course and mouth # From Tibet to Vietnam’s delta. Seasonal cycle and floods # Flood pulse reverses Cambodia’s Tonlé Sap river each year. Flora and fauna # Mekong giant catfish, giant freshwater stingray, Irrawaddy dolphins. People # About 60 million people depend on its fish. Threats # Over 100 dams, sand mining, sinking delta.

d: India's sacred river, forming with the Brahmaputra the world's largest delta.
x: Course and mouth # From the Gangotri Glacier across the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the Sundarbans. Seasonal cycle and floods # Monsoon floods supply most of its flow. Flora and fauna # Ganges river dolphin, gharial, Ganges shark, hilsa, mahseer. People # Over 500 million people in its basin. Threats # Pollution, dams and barrages (Farakka), groundwater loss.

d: A braided giant flowing from Tibet through Assam and Bangladesh.
x: Course and mouth # Called Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet; carves one of the deepest canyons on Earth. Seasonal cycle and floods # Monsoon floods and huge sediment loads. Flora and fauna # Ganges river dolphin, golden mahseer, Kaziranga floodplain wildlife. People # Assam and Bangladesh. Threats # Proposed dams, erosion.

d: Cradle of the Harappan civilisation.
x: Course and mouth # From Tibet through Ladakh and Pakistan. Seasonal cycle and floods # Snowmelt and monsoon floods (2022 floods). Flora and fauna # Indus river dolphin (blind), palla fish. People # Pakistan’s agriculture. Threats # Delta starved of water and sediment.

d: India's second-longest river, the 'Dakshin Ganga'.
x: Course and mouth # Across the Deccan Plateau to a delta in Andhra Pradesh. Seasonal cycle and floods # Monsoon floods. Flora and fauna # Mangroves at Coringa, olive ridleys nearby. People # Farming in the delta. Threats # Dams, pollution.

d: Odisha's great river, feeding Chilika Lake area and the Bhitarkanika mangroves.
x: Course and mouth # Flows from Chhattisgarh through Hirakud Dam to Odisha. Seasonal cycle and floods # Monsoon floods. Flora and fauna # Saltwater crocodiles and olive ridleys near its delta. People # Odisha agriculture and Hirakud. Threats # Industrial pollution, coal mining.

d: A major Deccan river with mangroves at its mouth.
x: Course and mouth # From the Western Ghats to Andhra Pradesh. Seasonal cycle and floods # Monsoon flow. Flora and fauna # Fishing cats, mangroves. People # Irrigation. Threats # Over-abstraction.

d: A west-flowing rift-valley river sacred in central India.
x: Course and mouth # Through marble gorges at Bhedaghat. Seasonal cycle and floods # Monsoon floods. Flora and fauna # Mahseer, hilsa near the estuary. People # Sardar Sarovar Dam. Threats # Dams reducing flow to the estuary.

d: Myanmar's lifeline, home of the Irrawaddy dolphin.
x: Course and mouth # North to south through Myanmar. Seasonal cycle and floods # Monsoon floods. Flora and fauna # Irrawaddy dolphins that cooperate with fishers. People # Rice farming. Threats # Mining, dams.

d: Africa's fourth-longest river, plunging over Victoria Falls.
x: Course and mouth # Through Zambia, Zimbabwe and Mozambique. Seasonal cycle and floods # Seasonal floods; Kariba and Cahora Bassa dams. Flora and fauna # Hippos, crocodiles, tigerfish. People # Hydropower. Threats # Dams altering delta mangroves.

d: Flows in a boomerang through the Sahel to a vast oil-rich delta.
x: Course and mouth # Inner Niger Delta wetlands in Mali. Seasonal cycle and floods # Seasonal flood pulses. Flora and fauna # West African manatees, hippos. People # Fisheries, oil. Threats # Oil spills in the delta.

d: Europe's second-longest river, flowing through 10 countries.
x: Course and mouth # From the Black Forest to a large delta in Romania. Seasonal cycle and floods # Spring snowmelt floods. Flora and fauna # Danube delta pelicans, beluga sturgeon migrations (blocked by dams). People # Major waterway. Threats # Dams, pollution.

d: Europe's longest river.
x: Course and mouth # Through Russia to the Caspian delta. Seasonal cycle and floods # Spring floods. Flora and fauna # Beluga sturgeon (caviar). People # Russian heartland. Threats # Dams blocking sturgeon.

d: Western Europe's busiest waterway.
x: Course and mouth # From the Alps through the Netherlands. Seasonal cycle and floods # Snowmelt and rain floods. Flora and fauna # Atlantic salmon being restored. People # Industry and shipping. Threats # Past pollution (Sandoz 1986).

d: London's river, once declared biologically dead (1957), now home to seals.
x: Course and mouth # Estuary into the North Sea. Seasonal cycle and floods # Tidal; Thames Barrier protects London. Flora and fauna # Seals, seahorses, eels. People # London. Threats # Sewage overflows.

d: Outlet of the Great Lakes, with one of the world's largest estuaries.
x: Course and mouth # From Lake Ontario to the Atlantic. Seasonal cycle and floods # Seasonal ice. Flora and fauna # Belugas, blue whales in the estuary. People # Shipping seaway. Threats # Pollution affecting belugas.

d: Historically the greatest salmon river on Earth.
x: Course and mouth # From British Columbia to Oregon. Seasonal cycle and floods # Snowmelt floods. Flora and fauna # Chinook and sockeye salmon, Pacific lamprey. People # Hydropower dams. Threats # Dams blocking salmon.

d: Home to one of the longest salmon migrations.
x: Course and mouth # From Canada through Alaska. Seasonal cycle and floods # Ice breakup. Flora and fauna # Chinook and chum salmon. People # Indigenous fisheries. Threats # Salmon declines.

d: Venezuela's great river with a vast delta.
x: Course and mouth # Connected to the Amazon by the Casiquiare channel. Seasonal cycle and floods # Floods. Flora and fauna # Orinoco crocodile, river dolphins. People # Llanos ranching. Threats # Mining.

d: South America's second-largest river.
x: Course and mouth # Forms the Río de la Plata estuary. Seasonal cycle and floods # Floods. Flora and fauna # Franciscana dolphins in the estuary. People # Itaipu Dam. Threats # Drought, dams.

d: Australia's largest river system.
x: Course and mouth # Ends at the Coorong lagoons. Seasonal cycle and floods # Highly variable flow. Flora and fauna # Murray cod. People # Irrigation. Threats # Over-extraction, fish kills.

d: High-rainfall river of New Guinea.
x: Course and mouth # Delta into the Gulf of Papua. Seasonal cycle and floods # Steady flow. Flora and fauna # Pig-nosed turtle. People # Mining. Threats # Ok Tedi mine tailings.

d: Forms the Pearl River Delta megacity region.
x: Course and mouth # Estuary between Hong Kong and Macau. Seasonal cycle and floods # Monsoon floods. Flora and fauna # Chinese white dolphins. People # Over 80 million people. Threats # Pollution, reclamation.

d: The world's muddiest major river.
x: Course and mouth # Through the Loess Plateau. Seasonal cycle and floods # Historic catastrophic floods. Flora and fauna # Migratory birds at the delta. People # Cradle of Chinese civilisation. Threats # Dry spells when it fails to reach the sea.

d: Forms much of the Russia–China border.
x: Course and mouth # Into the Tatar Strait. Seasonal cycle and floods # Summer monsoon floods. Flora and fauna # Kaluga sturgeon, salmon. People # Fisheries. Threats # Pollution.

d: The twin rivers of Mesopotamia.
x: Course and mouth # Join as the Shatt al-Arab. Seasonal cycle and floods # Spring floods. Flora and fauna # Mesopotamian marshes’ birds and fish. People # Cradle of civilisation. Threats # Dams, drought, salinisation.

d: South India's sacred river, famous for mahseer.
x: Course and mouth # From Coorg to Tamil Nadu’s delta. Seasonal cycle and floods # Monsoon flow. Flora and fauna # Hump-backed mahseer. People # Rice delta. Threats # Water disputes.

d: Ganges distributary on which Kolkata stands.
x: Course and mouth # Through West Bengal to the Bay. Seasonal cycle and floods # Tidal bore. Flora and fauna # Ganges dolphins, hilsa. People # Kolkata port. Threats # Pollution.

d: The 'unsinkable' liner that sank on its maiden voyage after striking an iceberg; ~1,500 died.
x: How it sank # Struck an iceberg on 14 April 1912 and sank in under three hours; too few lifeboats led to new safety rules (SOLAS 1914). How it was found # Found by Robert Ballard and Jean-Louis Michel in 1985 using the towed camera sled Argo; a full 3D scan was made in 2022–23. What we learned # Iron-eating bacteria (Halomonas titanicae) form ‘rusticles’ that are slowly consuming the hull.

d: Shackleton's ship, crushed by sea ice; all 28 men survived after an epic escape.
x: How it sank # Trapped in Weddell Sea ice in 1915 and crushed; Shackleton sailed 1,300 km in an open boat to South Georgia to get help. How it was found # Found in 2022 by the Endurance22 expedition with Sabertooth underwater robots, remarkably intact. What we learned # No wood-boring shipworms in Antarctic waters, so the wood is preserved.

d: Flagship of the lost Franklin expedition searching for the Northwest Passage.
x: How it sank # Both ships were abandoned in ice; all 129 men died. How it was found # Found in 2014 by Parks Canada guided by Inuit oral history; HMS Terror was found in 2016. What we learned # Shows how Indigenous knowledge solved a 170-year mystery.

d: Franklin's second ship, found almost intact in 2016.
x: How it sank # Abandoned with Erebus in 1848. How it was found # Located after a tip from an Inuk crew member. What we learned # Ice-cold water preserves artefacts.

d: A Swedish warship that capsized on its maiden voyage, raised almost intact in 1961.
x: How it sank # Top-heavy design; it sank less than 1.5 km into its first trip. How it was found # Found by Anders Franzén in 1956; now in Stockholm’s Vasa Museum. What we learned # The Baltic’s low salinity excludes shipworms.

d: Henry VIII's flagship that sank in battle against the French.
x: How it sank # Heeled over and flooded through open gunports. How it was found # Raised in 1982; its preserved half-hull is in Portsmouth. What we learned # Thousands of Tudor artefacts.

d: Contained the Antikythera mechanism, an ancient Greek astronomical computer.
x: How it sank # Sank around 60 BCE carrying luxury goods. How it was found # Found by sponge divers in 1900. What we learned # The mechanism predicted eclipses with bronze gears.

d: A 3,300-year-old ship carrying copper, tin, glass and gold from many cultures.
x: How it sank # Late Bronze Age trading vessel. How it was found # Found by a sponge diver in 1982; excavated 1984–94. What we learned # Evidence of Bronze Age global trade.

d: The oldest intact shipwreck known, ~2,400 years old.
x: How it sank # A trading vessel lost in deep water. How it was found # Found by the Black Sea Maritime Archaeology Project with ROVs. What we learned # Anoxic water preserved it perfectly.

d: The 'holy grail of shipwrecks', possibly carrying billions in gold and silver.
x: How it sank # Sunk by the British in the War of the Spanish Succession. How it was found # Found by Colombia with REMUS AUVs in 2015. What we learned # Ownership disputed between Colombia, Spain and Indigenous groups.

d: Germany's mighty battleship sunk after a chase across the Atlantic.
x: How it sank # Sunk by the Royal Navy three days after sinking HMS Hood. How it was found # Found by Robert Ballard in 1989. What we learned # Debate over scuttling versus gunfire.

d: Torpedoed after delivering atomic bomb parts; many survivors died from sharks and exposure.
x: How it sank # Sank in 12 minutes; ~316 of 1,195 survived. How it was found # Found by Paul Allen’s RV Petrel in 2017. What we learned # Shark attacks on survivors were among the worst recorded.

d: The deepest shipwreck ever surveyed by crewed submersible (2021).
x: How it sank # Sunk in the Battle off Samar. How it was found # Surveyed by Victor Vescovo in Limiting Factor. What we learned # Demonstrates full-depth submersibles.

d: The largest battleship ever built, sunk by US aircraft.
x: How it sank # Sunk on a one-way mission to Okinawa. How it was found # Located in 1985. What we learned # War grave.

d: Torpedoed by a German U-boat, helping bring the US into WWI.
x: How it sank # Sank in 18 minutes; 1,198 died. How it was found # Located in 1935. What we learned # Second explosion still debated.

d: A famous dive site filled with WWII motorbikes, trucks and trains.
x: How it sank # Bombed by German aircraft. How it was found # Found by Jacques Cousteau. What we learned # Now an artificial reef.

d: Over 50 ships sunk in Operation Hailstone, now a reef-covered underwater museum.
x: How it sank # US air raid on the Japanese base. How it was found # Explored by Cousteau’s team in 1969. What we learned # Leaking fuel is a pollution risk.

d: Wrecked off Australia, followed by a notorious mutiny and massacre.
x: How it sank # Ran aground on a reef. How it was found # Located in 1963; hull in Fremantle. What we learned # Early contact between Europeans and Australia.

d: The largest ship lost on the Great Lakes, in a November storm.
x: How it sank # Sank with all 29 crew. How it was found # Found days later by aircraft magnetometer. What we learned # Freshwater preservation.

d: A 9th-century Arab ship carrying ~60,000 Chinese ceramics.
x: How it sank # Evidence of the maritime Silk Road. How it was found # Found by sea-cucumber divers. What we learned # Ethics of commercial salvage debated.

d: Offshore stone structures off Dwarka linked by some to the legendary city.
x: How it sank # Ancient coastal settlement remains. How it was found # Surveyed by the National Institute of Oceanography (S.R. Rao) from 1983. What we learned # Dating and interpretation are debated.

d: Structures revealed after the 2004 tsunami shifted sand.
x: How it sank # Possibly linked to the legend of the Seven Pagodas. How it was found # Surveyed by NIO and the Scientific Exploration Society in 2002 and after 2004. What we learned # Shows coastal change.

d: The 'Indian Titanic': torpedoed with ~958 people aboard, many Indian passengers.
x: How it sank # Sunk by a Japanese submarine; 280 died. How it was found # Located in 2017 by salvors recovering its silver. What we learned # Remembrance of a little-known tragedy.

d: Italian liner sunk after a collision; the 'Mount Everest of wreck diving'.
x: How it sank # Collided with MS Stockholm in fog. How it was found # Sank the next day; 46 died. What we learned # Dangerous dive site.

d: Titanic's sister ship, sunk by a mine in WWI.
x: How it sank # Sank in 55 minutes; 30 died. How it was found # Found by Cousteau in 1975. What we learned # Largest intact passenger ship wreck.

d: The only authenticated pirate shipwreck, captained by 'Black Sam' Bellamy.
x: How it sank # Wrecked in a storm. How it was found # Found by Barry Clifford in 1984. What we learned # Pirate life artefacts.

d: A Swedish flagship that exploded in battle.
x: How it sank # Capsized and its magazine exploded. How it was found # Found in 1980. What we learned # Rich 17th-century artefacts.

d: A 16th-century Swedish flagship, among the best-preserved of its age.
x: How it sank # Sank in battle. How it was found # Found in 2011. What we learned # Baltic preservation.

d: The 'Ship of Gold' whose loss helped trigger the Panic of 1857.
x: How it sank # Sank in a hurricane carrying California gold. How it was found # Found using sonar and statistical search theory (Bayesian search). What we learned # Pioneered deep-sea search methods.

d: The largest underwater search ever, which mapped ~120,000 km² of unknown seafloor.
x: How it sank # Aircraft disappeared on 8 March 2014. How it was found # Not found; renewed searches in 2018 and 2025. What we learned # The search revealed new seafloor features in great detail.

d: Most ocean waves are made by wind transferring energy to the water surface.
x: How it forms # Wind friction creates capillary ripples, which give the wind more grip; waves grow with wind speed, duration and fetch (distance). Water particles move in circles, so energy travels but water mostly stays in place. Waves break when height exceeds about one-seventh of the wavelength or when they reach depths of ~1.3 times their height. Effects # Shape beaches and coasts, mix the upper ocean, drive surf. Key numbers # Significant wave height is measured by buoys and satellite altimeters; ~30 m waves have been recorded in storms.

d: The tiniest waves, controlled by surface tension rather than gravity.
x: How it forms # When wind first touches calm water, surface tension acts as a restoring force, making ripples shorter than ~1.7 cm. They give later waves a rougher surface to grow on. Sand ripples on the seabed form separately as currents and waves move sand grains. Effects # Start the wave-growth process; sand ripples record past currents in rocks. Key numbers # Ripple speed is a minimum (~23 cm/s) at ~1.7 cm wavelength.

d: Waves that have left the storm that made them and travel across ocean basins.
x: How it forms # Long-period waves outrun short ones and sort themselves into smooth swell, losing little energy over thousands of km. Effects # Surf, coastal erosion, ship motion. Key numbers # Swell periods of 15–25 s.

d: Unexpectedly huge waves more than twice the surrounding wave height.
x: How it forms # Waves add together constructively, and nonlinear focusing can pile energy into one giant wave; currents opposing waves (e.g. Agulhas) increase risk. Effects # Sink or damage ships. Key numbers # The Draupner wave (1995, 25.6 m) was the first measured; the Ucluelet wave (2020) was nearly 3× the background.

d: Long waves set off by sudden seafloor movement, landslides or volcanoes.
x: How it forms # An earthquake lifts the seafloor and the water above it. In deep water the wave is low but travels at ~700–800 km/h; near shore it slows and grows tall. Effects # The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed ~230,000; Tōhoku 2011 killed ~18,000. Key numbers # DART buoys detect pressure changes on the seabed.

d: The regular rise and fall of the sea caused by the Moon and Sun.
x: How it forms # The Moon’s gravity pulls water into two bulges; Earth spins under them. Spring tides occur at new and full moon when Sun and Moon align; neap tides at quarter moons. Coastline shape amplifies tides. Effects # Intertidal habitats, tidal power, navigation. Key numbers # Tide gauges since the 1800s also track sea-level rise.

d: A wall of water that travels up a river as the tide floods in.
x: How it forms # A large tidal range funnelled into a narrowing estuary. Effects # Dangerous for boats; surfed by enthusiasts. Key numbers # Qiantang bore reaches ~9 m.

d: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are giant storms powered by warm ocean water.
x: How it forms # Sea surface above ~26.5°C fuels evaporation; rising moist air releases heat as it condenses, lowering pressure and drawing in more air. Earth’s rotation (Coriolis effect) makes it spin, so cyclones cannot form at the equator. Low wind shear lets the vertical structure build. An eye forms where air sinks at the centre. Effects # Wind, storm surge, flooding rain; a warmer ocean makes the strongest storms stronger and wetter. Key numbers # About 80–90 tropical cyclones form each year worldwide.

d: The rise in sea level pushed ashore by a storm's winds and low pressure.
x: How it forms # Onshore winds pile water against the coast; low pressure lifts the sea ~1 cm per hPa; shallow funnel-shaped bays amplify it. Effects # The 1970 Bhola cyclone surge killed ~300,000 in Bangladesh. Key numbers # Surges can exceed 8 m.

d: A seasonal reversal of winds that brings the rainy season to South Asia and beyond.
x: How it forms # In summer, land heats faster than the ocean, creating low pressure that draws moist ocean air inland; in winter the pattern reverses. Effects # India receives ~70–80% of its rainfall from the southwest monsoon. Key numbers # Onset over Kerala around 1 June.

d: The biggest natural swing in Earth's climate, centred on the tropical Pacific.
x: How it forms # Normally trade winds push warm water west. In El Niño they weaken, warm water spreads east and upwelling off Peru shuts down; La Niña strengthens the normal state. Effects # El Niño raises global temperature, brings drought to India and Australia and floods to Peru; triggers coral bleaching. Key numbers # Tracked with the Oceanic Niño Index.

d: A see-saw of sea temperature between the western and eastern Indian Ocean.
x: How it forms # Positive phase: warmer west, cooler east; negative is the reverse. Effects # Positive IOD boosts Indian monsoon rains and East African floods; drives Australian droughts and fires (2019). Key numbers # Dipole Mode Index.

d: Cold, nutrient-rich deep water rising to the surface, fuelling the richest fisheries.
x: How it forms # Along-shore winds plus Earth’s rotation push surface water offshore (Ekman transport), and deep water rises to replace it. Effects # Upwelling zones cover ~1% of the ocean but give ~20% of the fish catch. Key numbers # Seen as cold, green water in satellite images.

d: Huge rotating current systems in each ocean basin.
x: How it forms # Driven by trade winds and westerlies plus the Coriolis effect, with fast western boundary currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio). Effects # Concentrate floating plastic (the ‘garbage patches’). Key numbers # The North Atlantic Gyre encloses the Sargasso Sea.

d: The global conveyor belt driven by differences in temperature and salt.
x: How it forms # Cold, salty water sinks in the North Atlantic and around Antarctica, spreads through the deep ocean, and slowly rises elsewhere. Effects # Distributes heat, oxygen and carbon; the AMOC is its Atlantic branch. Key numbers # Water takes ~1,000 years to complete a circuit.

t: Ekman transport and the Coriolis effect
d: Why ocean currents turn right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern.
x: How it forms # Earth’s rotation deflects moving water; wind-driven surface layers move at an angle to the wind, net transport 90° to it. Effects # Explains upwelling, gyres and cyclone spin. Key numbers # Named after Walfrid Ekman (1905).

d: Narrow, fast currents flowing away from the beach.
x: How it forms # Breaking waves pile water on shore; it escapes seaward through gaps in sandbars. Effects # The leading surf-beach hazard; swim parallel to shore to escape. Key numbers # Speeds up to ~2.5 m/s.

d: Huge waves inside the ocean between layers of different density.
x: How it forms # Tides flowing over ridges disturb density layers, making waves that can be 100 m+ high but invisible at the surface. Effects # Mix the ocean, move nutrients, affect submarines. Key numbers # Visible from space as surface slicks.

d: Swirling whirlpools of water that break off from currents.
x: How it forms # Instabilities in strong currents pinch off rings of warm or cold water. Effects # Carry heat, nutrients and larvae; Agulhas rings leak Indian Ocean water into the Atlantic. Key numbers # Tracked by satellite altimetry.

d: Powerful rotating tidal currents.
x: How it forms # Strong tides flowing through narrow straits create vortices. Effects # Navigation hazards and legends. Key numbers # Saltstraumen currents reach ~40 km/h.

d: Periods of unusually warm ocean water, now becoming more frequent and intense.
x: How it forms # Weak winds, high pressure and ocean heat build-up allow surface water to stay abnormally warm. Effects # Coral bleaching, kelp loss, seabird and fish die-offs. Key numbers # Have roughly doubled in frequency since the 1980s.

d: Global sea level is rising as ice melts and warming water expands.
x: How it forms # Thermal expansion plus melting glaciers and ice sheets; local land subsidence adds to it. Effects # Coastal flooding, saltwater intrusion, threat to atoll nations. Key numbers # ~21 cm since 1900, accelerating to over 4 mm a year.

d: How the polar oceans freeze and why it matters.
x: How it forms # Seawater freezes at about −1.8°C; ice crystals form frazil and pancake ice that consolidate. Salt is rejected, making dense water that sinks. Effects # Habitat for algae, krill, seals and bears; reflects sunlight; drives deep-water formation. Key numbers # Satellite records since 1979.

t: The water cycle and the ocean
d: The ocean is the source of most rain and the end of most rivers.
x: How it forms # About 86% of global evaporation comes from the ocean; most falls back over the sea, the rest over land, returning via rivers and groundwater. Effects # Drives weather; ocean salinity patterns record the cycle intensifying with warming. Key numbers # About 1.3 billion km³ of water are in the ocean, ~97% of Earth’s water.

d: Areas where oxygen is too low for most marine life.
x: How it forms # Nutrient runoff fuels algal blooms; bacteria decomposing them use up oxygen in stratified water. Effects # Over 500 coastal dead zones are known. Key numbers # Gulf of Mexico dead zone averages ~14,000 km².

d: Explosive growth of toxic algae that discolour the water.
x: How it forms # Warm water, nutrients and calm conditions favour blooms of dinoflagellates and diatoms. Effects # Fish kills, shellfish poisoning, respiratory irritation. Key numbers # Karenia brevis blooms in Florida.

d: Glowing waters caused by light-producing plankton and bacteria.
x: How it forms # Dinoflagellates flash when disturbed; ‘milky seas’ are vast areas lit steadily by bacteria (Vibrio). Effects # Tourism; milky seas are seen by satellite. Key numbers # A 2019 milky sea covered ~100,000 km².

d: Rotating columns of air and mist over water.
x: How it forms # Fair-weather waterspouts form under developing cumulus; tornadic ones descend from thunderstorms. Effects # Hazard to boats. Key numbers # Typically last 5–10 minutes.

d: Clouds of mineral-laden hot water rising from seafloor vents.
x: How it forms # Seawater heated by magma rises and mixes, spreading metals and nutrients for hundreds of km. Effects # Supply iron to the ocean. Key numbers # Plumes detected over 4,000 km from vents.

d: Underwater avalanches of sediment racing down slopes.
x: How it forms # Earthquakes or floods destabilise sediment that flows downslope faster than the water. Effects # Broke transatlantic cables in 1929 (Grand Banks); carry microplastics to the deep. Key numbers # Speeds up to ~70 km/h.

d: 'Icicles of death' growing down from sea ice into the water.
x: How it forms # Cold, salty brine leaking from sea ice freezes seawater around it as it sinks. Effects # Can trap and freeze bottom-dwelling animals. Key numbers # First filmed in 2011.
